British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
The impact of an
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    ‐driven multimodal teaching analytics dashboard on pre‐service teachers' reflective learning in microteaching
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Microteaching is a cornerstone of teacher education, enabling pre‐service teachers (PSTs) to rehearse, observe and refine instructional practices through structured reflection. Traditional video‐based review in microteaching is often time‐consuming and insufficiently analytical. Although learning analytics dashboards (LADs) can visualize teaching data to support reflection, many remain descriptive, offering limited insight into how behavioural evidence relates to pedagogical meaning. To address this gap, this study introduces iTeachBoard, an AI‐driven multimodal teaching analytics dashboard that integrates layered multimodal timeline visualization based on data‐storytelling design principle with LLM‐generated narrative feedback to support reflective learning in microteaching. A quasi‐experimental study (
                    n
                     = 53) compared iTeachBoard with a conventional visual analytics dashboard (VAD). Results revealed that iTeachBoard significantly enhanced PSTs' data interpretation, meaning construction and reflective writing depth. Participants perceived narrative‐style feedback as more trustworthy, explainable and pedagogically relevant. These findings suggest that LLM‐driven multimodal learning analytics can help bridge data visualization and pedagogical interpretation, thereby supporting PSTs' sense‐making, particularly data interpretation and meaning construction, as well as reflective writing depth in microteaching.
                  
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            Microteaching offers pre‐service teachers (PSTs) valuable opportunities to rehearse lessons, receive feedback and reflect on their teaching. However, reflections often remain superficial due to limited feedback structure and lack of actionable guidance.
                          
                          
                            Learning analytics dashboards (LADs) can visualize teaching behaviours, but most rely on descriptive metrics that lack interpretability and pedagogical relevance.
                          
                          
                            Sense‐making and data‐storytelling design principles have been proposed to help PSTs connect learning data with pedagogical meaning, yet empirical validation in teacher education remains scarce.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            Introduces iTeachBoard, an AI‐driven multimodal LAD that integrates large language model (LLM)‐based narrative feedback with multimodal visualizations to support deep reflective learning in microteaching.
                          
                          
                            Proposes the AI for Microteaching Multimodal Analytics Model (AI4MT), linking observable teaching behaviours to pedagogically meaningful reflective dimensions.
                          
                          
                            Provides empirical evidence that narrative‐style feedback combined with multimodal visualization significantly improves PSTs' overall sense‐making, with significant gains in data interpretation and meaning construction, as well as reflective writing depth, compared with a conventional video analytics dashboard.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and/or policy
                        
                          
                            iTeachBoard can be implemented in teacher education and professional development to promote evidence‐based reflection, collaborative lesson analysis and continuous pedagogical improvement.
                          
                          
                            The dashboard can enhance teachers' data literacy and AI literacy, fostering meaningful engagement with multimodal feedback for reflective growth.
                          
                          
                            Institutions should develop policies ensuring ethical data use, privacy protection and transparency in AI‐supported reflective systems to promote responsible adoption in educational settings.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
<scp>GenAI</scp>
                    ‐based metacognitive prompting in collaborative inquiry: A comparison across diverse preconception groups
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into collaborative inquiry to provide metacognitive prompting that scaffolds socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL). Understanding how such GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting is taken up through student–GenAI interactions is therefore critical. However, although learner–GenAI interaction processes have been widely examined, little is known about how learners' preconceptions shape their engagement with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting. This study examined how groups with different or similar preconceptions about energy forms and conservation differed in their engagement with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting during collaborative inquiry. Participants comprised 14 small groups, including eight groups with different preconceptions (D groups) and six groups with similar preconceptions (S groups). The distribution of learner‐generated inquiries directed to the written metacognitive AI (MAI) was largely comparable across groups. Lag sequential analysis revealed contrasting patterns in how groups evaluated the metacognitive prompts: D groups showed sustained positive or neutral evaluation of the prompts, whereas S groups showed sustained negative evaluation. Process mining further showed that AI query negotiation served as a hub in D groups' collaboration, connecting their conceptual discussions and task coordination. In S groups, by contrast, it formed part of a simpler, linear sequence of querying the AI and processing its responses. This study advances understanding of how preconception diversity shapes the processes and dynamics of human–AI collaboration. The findings show that AI‐mediated regulation varies depending on group‐level knowledge configurations.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Effective collaborative inquiry depends on learners' prior knowledge resources and their regulatory capacity.
                            
                            
                              Preconceptions, as a core component of prior knowledge, shape how learners interpret problems and engage in conceptual discussion.
                            
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting is designed to externalise metacognitive awareness and scaffold learners' regulatory processes.
                            
                            
                              Regulation unfolds through temporally ordered interaction sequences that reveal underlying regulatory dynamics.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              This study compares how different preconception groups and similar preconception groups engage with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting during collaborative scientific inquiry.
                            
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting responded to similar types of learner inquiries across groups.
                            
                            
                              GenAI query interaction in different preconception groups appeared more integrated with conceptual and task discussion, whereas in similar preconception groups it followed a more linear, output‐focused path.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting may benefit from incorporating a preliminary classification layer that distinguishes between metacognitive prompts and procedural or informational requests.
                            
                            
                              Teachers may consider preconception diversity when forming groups, as different epistemic configurations appear to give rise to distinct patterns of GenAI‐learner collaboration.
                            
                            
                              Policymakers and designers should recognise that GenAI functions as a co‐regulator within collaborative settings, and its impact depends on how it is interactionally integrated into group interactional trajectories.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    as a team moderator in
                    <scp>CSCL</scp>
                    : Facilitating students' multidimensional engagement through adaptive scaffolding for socially shared regulation of learning
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is essential for successful collaboration, yet effectively scaffolding it remains challenging because regulatory needs are dynamic and context‐dependent. While generative AI (GenAI) offers potential for adaptive support, current applications in collaborative learning largely position it as a content‐oriented tutor for knowledge explanation or idea generation, leaving its role as a process‐oriented team moderator for scaffolding SSRL processes underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 16‐week quasi‐experiment with 64 undergraduates in China, comparing adaptive SSRL scaffolding delivered by a GenAI agent in the adaptive‐SSRL condition with static scaffolding via structured digital worksheets in the static‐SSRL condition. Survey data and group discussion transcripts were analysed using statistical methods and epistemic network analysis. Results indicated several differences in students' multidimensional engagement between the two conditions: (1) Behaviourally, the adaptive‐SSRL group showed significantly higher participation equality, although participation intensity did not differ significantly between groups. (2) Cognitively, the adaptive‐SSRL group demonstrated deeper cognitive engagement, reflected in more advanced cognitive presence phases and more integrative, solution‐oriented discourse patterns. (3) Emotionally, the adaptive‐SSRL group reported significantly higher overall emotional engagement, particularly feeling more relaxed during collaboration and more connected with peers. These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by showing that GenAI can function as an SSRL‐informed team moderator rather than a content‐oriented tutor. They also offer design implications for GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding and human–AI role division in CSCL.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is critical for successful collaboration and is closely associated with the quality of student engagement.
                            
                            
                              While static scaffolds (eg, worksheets) provide a basic regulatory structure, they fail to adapt to the dynamic and emergent needs of collaborating teams.
                            
                            
                              Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for personalised content support, yet its potential as a process‐oriented team moderator remains underexplored.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              This study introduced SSRLAgent, a GenAI agent grounded in SSRL theory and established principles of collective metacognitive support, to provide adaptive and interactive regulatory scaffolding.
                            
                            
                              In a 16‐week quasi‐experiment, we compared GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding (SSRLAgent) with static scaffolding (structured digital worksheets) in CSCL.
                            
                            
                              Adaptive‐SSRL scaffolding was associated with higher‐quality engagement: greater participation equality, deeper cognitive engagement and higher overall emotional engagement.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              The study underscores the necessity of shifting SSRL scaffolding from static, ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ support to adaptive GenAI interventions to improve collaborative engagement.
                            
                            
                              The findings provide design guidance for developing SSRL agents that are embedded in the shared interaction space and responsive to groups' moment‐to‐moment regulatory needs.
                            
                            
                              The study suggests a productive human–AI division of labour: GenAI agents can support process coordination and regulatory prompting, while teachers and peers remain essential for relationally complex forms of support that collaborative learning requires.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation.
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking.
                          
                          
                            Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes.
                          
                          
                            Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting.
                          
                          
                            Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT.
                          
                          
                            Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and/or policy
                        
                          
                            Prompt engineering can be used to simulate emotional support and personalize guidance based on SRL and emotion regulation principles, providing design considerations for future learner‐centred GenAI systems.
                          
                          
                            Developers and educators aiming to design pedagogically meaningful GenAI tools should focus on scaffolding SRL both cognitively and emotionally, to support the affective and self‐regulatory dimensions of learning.
                          
                          
                            We make the technical specifications and system prompts publicly available.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Mathematics in play: exploring curriculum integration and professional growth through playing, modelling and printing games
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  Integrating playful and maker-oriented approaches into mathematics teacher education remains challenging, particularly in relation to curricular alignment and teacher agency. This design-based research examines a workshop centred on the Hidden Blocks game, structured in three stages: play, digital modelling, and fabrication through 3D printing. The intervention was designed to support teachers’ mathematical reasoning, their articulation of links between the activity and the curriculum, and their professional agency as designers of resources and learning experiences. Across four cycles in Austria, Brazil, and Uruguay involving mathematics teachers, we analysed interviews, workshop recordings, facilitators’ notes, and lesson plans. Through iterative refinement, we developed a set of design principles organised into three interrelated dimensions: (a) mathematics, focusing on eliciting and formalising mathematical reasoning through play, modelling, and fabrication; (b) curriculum, focusing on explicit connections between mathematical ideas and curricular aims; and (c) professional agency, focusing on teachers’ ownership, authorship, and adaptation of resources for classroom use. These principles show how a technology-enhanced intervention that combines gameplay, modelling, and fabrication can support mathematisation, curriculum articulation, and teacher agency in mathematics teacher education.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Matching minds and materials: the interplay of learner support and learner characteristics
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  Prior knowledge is a central cognitive factor shaping how learners benefit from instructional support in digital learning environments. Pretraining and worked-out examples are known as single support strategies for activating or building prior knowledge and facilitating the integration of new knowledge. The interaction between prior knowledge and single support strategies has been widely studied. Yet the use of single support strategies does not reflect actual teaching practice, in which multiple forms of instructional support are tailored to learners’ characteristics so that all students can benefit effectively from instruction. This study examines the potential interaction between prior knowledge and the instructional support strategies of pretraining and worked-out examples, which can be applied sequentially when teaching adaptively. A total of 139 primary school students were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions in a 2 (pretraining vs. no pretraining) × 2 (partially vs. fully worked-out example) between-subjects factorial design, with prior knowledge as a moderator. Cognitive load and learning outcomes are examined. Results show that prior knowledge moderates learning outcomes, with lower prior knowledge learners profiting from both pretraining and worked-out examples. The higher the learners’ prior knowledge, the greater the effect shifted from positive to nonsignificant to negative. A significant three-way interaction emerged, indicating that the design of digital learning environments depends not only on learners’ prior knowledge but also on the combined influence of multiple support strategies. Practical implications point to the design of adaptive, technology-enhanced learning environments that dynamically tailor pretraining and worked-out examples to learners’ evolving knowledge states.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
Student Responses to Cognitive Conflicts in
                    <scp>GenAI</scp>
                    ‐Assisted Learning: A Covariate‐Dependent Markov Chain Analysis on Human‐
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Interactions
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reshapes the learning process, students will inevitably experience cognitive conflicts when their existing knowledge and beliefs clash with information provided by GenAI. Improper handling of cognitive conflicts may lead to a decline in students' learning efficiency and even hinder the development of critical thinking skills.
                  
                  
                    Objective
                    This study aims to understand how students respond to cognitive conflicts during their interactions with GenAI, with a focus on comparing high‐performing and low‐performing student groups.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    To identify relationships between cognitive conflict intensity and students' responses, we used a covariate‐dependent Markov chain (a sequential data modelling method) to analyse the response states of 411 students in a simulated academic writing task and observed transitions in student response states across different task performances.
                  
                  
                    Results
                    The results revealed that the intensity of cognitive conflict had a significant impact on students' state transitions. Overall, as the level of conflict increased, students' state changes exhibited a phased pattern, shifting from fluctuation (transitioning to a variety of different states) to inertia or convergence (maintaining the original state or transitioning uniformly to a negative response state). Student response state transitions varied across different task performance levels.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    This study provides a novel methodological perspective for modelling sequential response dynamics in Human‐AI interaction. The findings offer new insights into the cognitive conflict dynamics in GenAI‐assisted learning, providing implications for designing GenAI‐assisted learning environments.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
Impacts of
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    ‐Generated Learning Videos on Learning Outcomes: The Mediating Roles of Perceived Desirability and Perceived Feasibility
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    In recent educational research and practice, there has been growing attention to the use and impact of generative AI technologies, with most studies focusing on AI‐generated textual content. However, relatively little is known about AI‐generated learning videos, despite their potential to significantly influence learners' experiences and outcomes.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    Drawing on situational interest theory and construal level theory, this study investigates how three different types of AI‐generated learning videos influence learning outcomes through the mediating roles of perceived desirability and perceived feasibility. Three AI‐generated video types that represent ascending levels of learner involvement—situated videos, multiple‐choice interactive situated videos, and AI–learner co‐created videos—are examined.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    A between‐subjects experiment was conducted with 221 valid responses across four conditions: three AI‐generated learning video types and a traditional learning video control condition. ANOVA and partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM) were employed to validate the effects.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    Results show that all three types of AI‐generated videos significantly enhance learning outcomes—learning enjoyment, learning performance, and continuous learning intention—compared to traditional learning videos, with perceived feasibility mediating the effects on all three outcomes and perceived desirability mediating the effects on learning enjoyment and continuous learning intention. This study extends the theoretical boundaries of AI in learning research and provides actionable insights for teachers in instructional design.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: A Configurational Approach to Investigating the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Self‐Regulated Learning From Needs Satisfaction, Learning Environments and Perceived Affordances
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools into self‐regulated learning (SRL) is complex and multifaceted. Configurational approaches are based on the concept that combinations (or configurations) of causally relevant factors should be connected to the desired outcome.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    Self‐determination theory (SDT), the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) and perceived affordances focus on basic needs, technology adoptions and technological designs, respectively. Taking a configurational approach, this study investigates how the combinations of SDT, UTAUT and perceived affordances affect SRL with AI.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    We employed fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to uncover the complex interplay of factors that facilitate effective SRL. Data from 248 students reveal that a combination of autonomy satisfaction, relatedness satisfaction and performance expectancy is the most influential factor affecting the use of AI in SRL.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    Our results suggest that both innate psychological needs and external learning environments should be considered together for understanding the adoption of AI in SRL. They also further highlight the critical role of perceived affordances as mediators and moderators, enhancing the relationships between innate psychological needs and external learning environments. This integrative approach provides valuable insights into the design and implementation of AI‐supported SRL environments. We recommend designing the environments to foster autonomy and relatedness while also ensuring ease of use for learners.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
Designing Teaching Agents for Human‐
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Collaborative Classrooms: A Design‐Based Study of Students' Sense of Presence and Learning Engagement
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Generative artificial intelligence has expanded the possibilities for teaching agents to provide instructional explanations and feedback. However, limited research has examined how such support can be integrated into teacher‐guided classroom instruction and how students experience and engage with this form of teaching.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study aimed to iteratively design and refine teaching agents within a teacher‐guided undergraduate classroom and to examine changes in students' sense of presence and learning engagement across three design iterations.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    A single‐group design‐based research study was conducted in a 10‐week Introduction to Educational Technology course. 36 first‐year undergraduate students majoring in educational technology participated in three design iterations: gesture‐supported presentation, teacher‐mediated real‐time Q&A, and individualized text‐based Q&A. Data were collected through questionnaires, classroom observations, student feedback, question records, and discussion texts. Repeated‐measures analyses were used to examine changes in students' sense of presence and learning engagement, and epistemic network analysis was used to examine changes in co‐occurrence patterns among presence‐related codes in students' post‐class reflections.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    The findings show that students' sense of presence significantly increased across the three iterations, whereas learning engagement did not show a statistically significant change, although the descriptive means showed a small upward pattern. Epistemic network analysis identified changes in co‐occurrence patterns among presence‐related codes in students' post‐class reflections. The strongest connections involved direct instruction, affective expression, and resolution in the first iteration, and affective expression with direct instruction, exploration, and integration in the third iteration. Given the single‐group sequential design, these findings should be interpreted as observed changes during the iterative implementation process rather than causal evidence for the independent effects of specific design strategies. The study contributes process‐oriented evidence and design considerations for integrating teaching agents into teacher‐orchestrated human‐AI collaborative classrooms.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Comparing AI-Assisted 2D and 3D Block-Based Games for Computational Thinking Development in Introductory Programming
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Computational thinking (CT) is a foundational competency in undergraduate education, yet novice programmers frequently encounter high cognitive demands and declining motivation. Although block-based programming and AI-assisted scaffolding can reduce extraneous load by enabling natural-language interaction, it remains unclear whether embedding these capabilities within immersive three-dimensional environments further enhances CT development through reduced extraneous load and enriched spatial context for schema formation. This study employed a randomized between-subjects design to compare an AI-assisted 3D block-based game (CT Logic 3D) with an AI-assisted 2D counterpart (CT Logic 2D) over a four-week intervention involving fifty undergraduate students (
                    n
                    = 50, Mage = 23.3, SD = 1.07). Both conditions shared identical AI translation pipelines and instructional sequences, with spatial dimensionality constituting the sole experimental manipulation. Results indicated that participants in the 3D condition achieved significantly greater gains in CT (
                    d
                    = 0.54), stronger delayed retention (
                    d
                    = 0.74), and higher near-transfer problem-solving performance (
                    d
                    = 0.82). Relative to the 2D group, participants in the 3D condition completed tasks 22% faster (
                    d
                    = 1.08), reported lower perceived difficulty (
                    d
                    = 0.94), and experienced higher levels of flow (
                    d
                    = 0.89) and intrinsic motivation (
                    d
                    = 0.86). Engagement increased throughout the intervention, with the largest efficiency gains observed among absolute novices. Moreover, substantial rates of learner-initiated modification of AI-generated solutions (3D: 76%; 2D: 71%) indicated active rather than passive use of AI scaffolding. Interpreted through Cognitive Load Theory, the findings suggest that combining AI scaffolding with immersive spatial representations produces measurable advantages for CT development beyond those achievable through AI scaffolding alone. Theoretical and practical implications for the design of AI-enhanced CT instruction are discussed.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Developing and Validating an AI-Literacy-Integrated Teaching Acceptance and Readiness Scale for Mathematics Teachers
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
The global shift toward cultivating students’ AI literacy requires teachers to reconceptualize curricula and pedagogical practices. However, research has focused primarily on teachers’ use of AI tools, overlooking their readiness to integrate AI literacy as a learning goal, particularly in mathematics education. In response, this study developed and validated the AI-Literacy-Integrated Teaching Acceptance and Readiness Scale for Mathematics Teachers (AILTAR-M). The instrument was theoretically organized around two domains: (1)
                    Acceptance
                    , comprising four constructs adapted from the Technology Acceptance Model (Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, Attitude toward Use, and Behavioral Intention); and (2)
                    Readiness
                    , encompassing Perceived AI Literacy as a self-reported cognitive dimension and Teaching Self-Efficacy as a motivational dimension. Psychometric evaluation with 549 mathematics teachers in China supported a 29-item, six-factor structure. Exploratory factor analysis (
                    n
                    = 174) yielded a six-factor solution explaining 69.7% of the variance, and confirmatory factor analysis (
                    n
                    = 375) demonstrated acceptable model fit (CFI = .938, TLI = .931, RMSEA = .063, SRMR = .038). The instrument exhibited strong internal consistency (α = .899– .943) alongside satisfactory convergent and discriminant validity. These findings provide initial psychometric evidence for using the AILTAR-M to examine mathematics teachers’ acceptance of and readiness for integrating AI literacy into mathematics instruction.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Design and Evaluation of an Immersive VR Space Based on Pedagogical Agent for Theory of Mind Training in Autistic Children: Insights from Brain Activity and Participatory Study
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: While virtual reality (VR) offers potential for training children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), limited evidence guides pedagogical agent (PA) design for immersive theory of mind (ToM) training. This study adopted a sequential multi-method approach to develop and preliminarily evaluate a cave automatic virtual environment (CAVE)-based ToM training space for autistic children. Study 1 used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) with 22 autistic children and found that rich interaction elicited greater neural activation during ToM processing, particularly when anthropomorphic cues were limited. Building on these findings, Study 2 combined interviews with 6 autism education experts and a collage workshop with 8 autistic children. The integrated findings supported cartoon-style human agents with moderate facial expressions, low-saturation and limited colors, diverse movements, expressive speech, simple verbal expressions, stepwise cues, and contingent feedback. These strategies guided development of the CAVE-based training space in Study 3. The preliminary feasibility evaluation indicated satisfactory professional-user usability, with the three participating children showing higher post-training ToM scores and caregiver-reported changes in social functioning. Overall, the study provides design and methodological guidance for immersive learning environments that better align with autistic children’s processing characteristics and intervention needs, while suggesting the potential of the CAVE-based environment for ToM training.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Unraveling the Effects of Block-Based Visual Programming on Students’ Computational Thinking
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Nowadays, computational thinking has been the core necessary skill for students who want to succeed in the 21
                    st
                    century. Block-based visual programming (BBVP) is one of the most widely used ways to develop student computational thinking. However, its impact on student computational thinking is mixed in the education field. This study conducts a meta-analysis to compare the impacts of BBVP and textual programming on student computational thinking. The result covering 24 independent studies and 2,441 students indicates that BBVP has a large positive effect (
                    SMD
                    = 0.887,
                    CI
                    = [0.625, 1.148],
                    p
                    < 0.001) on student computational thinking. We also conduct moderator analysis and find that class size, treatment duration, test type, BBVP type, subject, learning method, and region significantly moderate BBVP’s impacts on students computational thinking. Finally, major findings, recommendations, and limitations are provided.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Toward an Interpretive Synthesis of Personalization, Co-Design, and Ethical Mediation in AI-Supported Higher Education: An Integrative Review of Agentic, Generative, and Adaptive Tutoring Systems
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies are expanding in higher education, raising questions about their alignment with pedagogical goals. This qualitative-integrative review synthesizes 57 publications (21 empirical, 25 conceptual or framework, 9 systematic reviews or meta-analyses retained for triangulation, and 2 design/development papers) from 2024 to 2026, employing Whittemore and Knafl’s methodology to examine AI-supported tutoring, implementation strategies, and learner/instructor experiences. Three interpretive themes organize this heterogeneous evidence: (1) personalization as a recurring target, from micro-level adaptation to curriculum design; (2) technology-pedagogy co-design as a recurring implementation pattern; and (3) contextual and ethical conditions surrounding adoption, including culture, policy gaps, well-being, and academic integrity. These themes are interpretive, not a validated framework, and draw on evidence of uneven strength. The present review does not estimate effect sizes or pool outcomes across studies; g = 0.70, reported by X. Wang et al. in a separate meta-analysis of 45 studies (2010–2022) of pre-generative adaptive systems, which is cited only as background, not as a finding of this review. Implications are framed as evidence-tiered hypotheses, while the layered model is offered as an interpretive scaffold for future research, not a confirmatory model.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: What counts as digital play? Irish early childhood educators’ beliefs and practice tensions
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Digital technologies are increasingly embedded in young children’s lives, yet uncertainty remains regarding their role in early childhood education and care (ECEC). This study explores Irish early years educators’ beliefs and perceptions concerning digital play, employing Bronfenbrenner’s bioecological framework to examine how policy, parental expectations and professional identity interact to shape children’s learning opportunities. Semi-structured interviews with 10 educators identified five themes: developmentalist beliefs prioritising ‘natural’ play, cautious openness to digital tools, professional identity and ethical tensions, perceptions of children and families and concerns about policy directives. Findings reveal a persistent policy–practice gap, where limited professional development and unclear guidance leave educators uncertain about how to define and implement quality digital play. The study emphasises that educators’ attitudes are closely associated with the extent and quality of children’s digital engagement, highlighting the need for sustained professional development and strengthened mesosystemic communication across home, school and policy contexts. Implications include the creation of context-sensitive frameworks that integrate digital and traditional play while supporting children’s holistic development. This study demonstrates that educators’ definitions of digital play are shaped by the interaction of professional identity, policy ambiguity, family expectations and resource conditions, offering new insight into the conditions that constrain digital play in Irish early years settings.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Teachers’ professional learning and development experiences in Chinese kindergartens: Opportunities and tensions
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Professional learning and development (PLD) activities for Chinese kindergarten teachers have introduced imported knowledge to promote teaching and learning. Much PLD provision is led by leaders and experts rather than teachers. To understand the educational beliefs and power differences that surface among teachers, leaders and experts during PLD sessions and how teachers navigate this complex terrain, this paper presents a post-intentional phenomenological study involving seven participants from two Chinese early childhood settings. Data collection included semi-structured interviews, observations of PLD meetings and videos of teachers’ implementation of PLD ideas. Educational policies, PLD materials, and the researcher’s reflexive journal were also used for analysis. Analysis involved a line-by-line reading process where theoretical concepts, data and researcher reflexivity interacted. The findings reveal that teachers experienced tensions in relation to formal PLD sessions. These tensions stemmed from established values and hierarchical constraints that limited their joint reflection and actions. Our analysis, framed by the concepts of relational agency and in-between spaces, shows how teachers navigated these tensions. Despite these constraints, the teachers responded by creating opportunities for collaborative learning. They sought out informal situations where they had the flexibility to develop shared knowledge. We argue that Chinese teachers’ PLD can occur within and across such tensions and opportunities. These informal situations empowered teachers to enact relational agency by aligning their expertise to make PLD decisions. This process eased tensions and created space for collaborative learning. The study concludes that valuing these informal, teacher-initiated spaces is crucial for moving beyond top-down knowledge transmission and fostering sustainable professional growth in hierarchical educational contexts. Ultimately, by empowering teachers as collaborative and adaptable professionals, this model of PLD offers new insights into enhancing the professional environments that shape teaching practice and young children’s learning.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Parent–school mobile communication in preschool: A qualitative study in Mexico
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: School-family communication in early childhood is increasingly mediated by mobile applications, yet important questions remain about what counts as high-quality content, how schools allocate topics between digital and face-to-face channels, and what costs these practices impose on teachers. This qualitative study examines how a mobile application shapes day-to-day parent-school communication in a Mexican preschool. Semi-structured interviews with four teachers and three mothers, combined with field observation, were thematically analyzed. The app supported timely and consistent exchanges about classroom life. Families valued brief, concrete descriptions of children’s socio-emotional participation, peer interactions, and strategies practiced, along with simple suggestions for follow-up at home. However, participants identified a depth gap when messages focused mainly on logistics, and teachers reported a workload tension between the burden of exhaustive daily reporting and the sense of security it provides to parents. A hybrid model of communication was preferred: routine updates and nonurgent questions were handled in the app, while complex, evaluative, or sensitive topics were addressed in planned one-to-one meetings. Reported short-term gains were primarily psychosocial, including higher trust and a closer working relationship between teachers and families. Findings support a shift from tool adoption to the quality of communicative practice in early childhood settings.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Promoting social skills and friendships in early childhood education: A case study of four children’s trajectories to inclusion
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: This paper reports on the changes reported on the social relations and skills of four children after the implementation of ProFriend (Promoting Friendship) in an early childhood education (ECE) setting. ProFriend is a programme developed considering the inclusive ECE principles by targeting all children’s access and participation and looking beyond imposed labels. The data of the study included friendship nominations, observations, children’s drawings, teachers’ interviews and research diary. The findings shed light on four children’s trajectories who faced challenges in forming friendships and whose individual characteristics (speech and language impairments and socio-emotional difficulties) were seen by teachers as barriers to their social development. The discussion focuses on how children’s exclusion can be minimised by enriching ECE curricula with some elements guiding teachers on how to approach the development of social skills and friendships in a meaningful and inclusive way.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: The impact of active transitions on preschool students’ self-regulation
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Early childhood education plays a pivotal role in fostering the holistic development of young learners through age-appropriate activities and interactions that support physical, social, emotional and cognitive growth. This study explored the relationship between active transitions in an early childhood education classroom and observable behaviour indicators of self-regulation in preschoolers, with a specific focus on the integration of yoga during transitional times. The objective was to investigate the impact of incorporating yoga on student self-regulation during large group literacy, as perceived by the preschool teacher. The research employed a collaborative action research design, engaging a preschool teacher in a reflective and systematic approach to improve classroom practices. Findings indicated that the integration of yoga, when including both challenging and sedentary poses, was associated with reductions in teacher-observed off-task behaviour during large group literacy, suggesting a possible positive influence on behaviour self-regulation. Results indicated that active transitions may support overall classroom management, increased instructional time and contributed to a comprehensive understanding of the effects of physical activity on young learners.

keyword_papers.title: Learning machine learning with young children: exploring informal settings in an African context
keyword_papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background and context Researchers have been investigating ways to demystify machine learning for students from kindergarten to twelfth grade (K–12) levels. As little evidence can be found in the literature, there is a need for additional research to understand and facilitate the learning experience of children while also considering the African context. Objective The purpose of this study was to explore how young children teach and develop their understanding of machine learning based technologies in playful and informal settings. Method Using a qualitative methodological approach through fine-grained analysis of video recordings and interviews, we analysed how 18 children aged 3–13 years constructed their interactions with a machine-based technology (Google’s Teachable Machine). Findings This study provides empirical support for the claim that Google’s Teachable Machine contributes to the development of data literacy and conceptual understanding across K–12 irrespective of the learners’ backgrounds. The results also confirmed children’s ability to infer the relationship between their own expressions and the output of the machine learning-based tool, thus, identifying the input-output relationships in machine learning. In addition, this study opens a discussion around differentials in emerging technology use across different contexts through participatory learning. Implications The results provide a baseline for future research on the topic and preliminary evidence to discern how children learn about machine learning in the African K–12 context.

keyword_papers.title: Clustering Young Children’s Coding Project Scores with Machine Learning
keyword_papers.abstract: Engaging children in making creative coding projects is a popular approach for young children to develop computational skills. Children learn to transform their ideas and knowledge into personally meaningful projects. However, the connection between children’s coding competencies and their created coding projects remains unclear. This study explored how ScratchJr coding projects created by first and second graders (n=75) differed and whether the project focuses varied by the children’s coding competencies. ScratchJr is a free downloadable tablet game for children ages 5-7 to create animated stories and games. Through unsupervised machine learning algorithms, this study grouped coding project concepts by Principal Component Analysis then classified students into four groups by K-means. The results showed that students across the four groups focused on creating different aspects of the ScratchJr projects. Moreover, the median coding competency score of each student group also differed significantly. This study implies that young children with varying levels of coding competency tend to focus on creating different aspects of ScratchJr projects. Findings from this study can help to inform curriculum designers and teachers on essential approaches for guiding children in creating their own coding projects.

keyword_papers.title: Applying Machine Learning to Support Adults in Educating 0- to 36-Month-Old Children at Home: Theories and Experience from Vietnam
keyword_papers.abstract: This research presents the theoretical bases and practical experiences in Vietnam in applying machine learning to support adults in educating 0- to 36-month-old children at home. The paper also reports the findings of a scientific research project named “Researching and applying machine learning to support adults to educate young children aged 0-36 months in their families” at Vietnam National University, Hanoi. To be more specific, the authors have designed an AI-driven chatbot which acts as a babysitter to provide information and answer frequently-asked questions regarding at-home education of 0- to 36-month-old children following prevalent scripts or data. For simple questions the AI-driven babysitter chatbot will offer the answers on their own. For more complex ones, the chatbot will send them to teachers for solutions. During the process, the chatbot will do self-learning to enhance its ability to give more accurate and practical answers. Experiments show that the chatbot designed by the authors has successfully addressed limitations of the conventional counterparts. Additionally, it also provides accurate and reliable answers, as well as enhanced user experience thanks to trusted references and parents’ coordination in effective child education, ensuring quality and authenticity.

keyword_papers.title: Learning machine learning with very young children: Who is teaching whom?
keyword_papers.abstract: Abstract While artificial intelligence and machine learning is becoming a commonplace feature of people’s everyday lives, so far few theoretical or empirical studies have focused on investigating it in K-12​ education. Drawing on the sociocultural theory of learning and participation, this case study explored how six very young children taught and explored Google’s Teachable Machine in nonschool settings. Through fine-grained analysis of video recordings and interviews with the children, the article illustrates the content and the process of teaching where 3–9 year old children were producing machine learning data sets and models as well as observing, exploring, and explaining their own interaction with machine learning systems. The results illustrate the quick-paced and embodied nature of the child-computer interaction that also supported children to reason about the relationship between their own bodily expressions and the output of an interactive ML-based tool. The article concludes with discussions on the emergent process of teaching and learning as well as on ways of promoting children’s participation and sense of agency in the age of machine learning.

keyword_papers.title: Introducing Machine Learning Through a Multisensory Approach for Young People with Down Syndrome
keyword_papers.abstract: This paper presents an ongoing educational activity to introduce Machine Learning concepts to children and young people with Down Syndrome. In Brazil, the lack of a standard for Computer Science Education until 2022 led to disparities, with public schools often lacking resources. A 2022 regulation made Computing mandatory in K-12, aligning with the Brazilian National Common Curricular Base, which includes Artificial Intelligence-related competencies. In the Brazilian context, Computing is still not part of the school curriculum for most students without disabilities. Students with developmental disorders, such as Down Syndrome, have even less access to activities designed to teach computational skills in their learning environments. However, it is possible to observe that, when provided with technologies adapted to their needs, these students can learn and develop effectively. Therefore, this work proposes a multisensory unplugged activity tailored to introduce Machine Learning concepts to people with Down Syndrome. Given the multisensory approach, we expect to observe benefits beyond computational learning, promoting the development of fine motor skills through a playful and fun experience.
